author: HCDE
text:
gslao wrote: HCDE,

I recall IF answering another student about the same question you had on
 "I have a very very hard time finding space, engulf not hitting its
target.". Yes, we need to find space otherwise, there is no trade. If
it was easy to find space, then everyone would become a successful
trader overnight. The ITs will not make it easy and obvious.

Trading is based on your preference and your comfort zone and your
confidence in your analysis. There are master traders who take touch
trades and take confirmation trade. It all depends on the trade itself.
 First, I would suggest you get comfortable with confirmation trades
before jumping to touch trade. Confirmation trades will provide you
more winners and put money in the bank for you. It will also build
your confidence. Touch trading can be tricky, so you need to read the
market correctly.... . You need to know if the level it is reacting to
is the true supply..... you need to know how it reacted when it reached
that level....., for example did price impulsive move away from that
level and engulf an important FL to its left without hitting TG. If so,
 you have PA.. Now you want to see how price is retracing and
approaching your entry point.(in this example, I am describing a
QM)...... is it compressing, is it compressing and then a final
impulsive move to your entry level....These are the questions that you
need to answer. The 1/2 page on article on price reading in Marketpedia
speaks it all. So, I would recommend you reading it over and over again
 until you truly understand. If you have any question, then you can
post them and other students will help answer.

Thanks for your answer, it helps me.

I end up having a good price reading skills, I think I got what are the
mecanisms behind left shoulders, i understand why there is symetry in
the market I understand the concepts and I think what is behind it. But
I'm really psychologically challenged by these confirmation trades.

I know myself, i'm cautious so I set myself a rule which is just take
confirmation trade. But I find so few of them that I get very very
psychologically challenged.

To be honest, I expected a lot of QM on one pair on small timeframes...

I think I'm gonna change the way I screen the market.

I used to take one or two pairs at a time and focus on them all day long. I think that's not working for me.

I'm gonna screen every pair I have every morning, asking myself: "Are we
 at a good HTF level or near that? If yes, monitor and wait for
confirmation, if no, go on..."

What about you guys, what is your trading routine?

author: Atari
text:
Here is a quote from IF. " The longer I trade, the fewer trades I
take. If it's not begging to be traded, I am not interested. There are
 lots of dead certain trades out there, each offering great returns.
These can easily be missed while sweating the outcome of marginal
trades."

For me, I prepare my trade plan a week in advance and look at the higher
 time frame down to the lower time frame to determine the IT price
direction. I keep my pairs to a maximum of 4. This helps me focus and
maximize my entry. Otherwise, I will end up missing the big trades.

author: Edge
text:
The further I stroll down this path, it becomes apparent that less is
more. Imagine for a minute, watching 20 plus pairs and trading for
limited R. How stressed and tired would you become.

On the flip side only watching a few pairs with low spread, waiting for
those beautiful areas that are a monthly kink that are only a few pips
wide. You then find a marvelous mpl within it with clean orders just
begging to be taken. We then see the eg of the opposing FL into space on
 the monthly and it returns to our kink and mpl. The R can be
phenominal.

The necessity to trade everyday feel the thrilland be in and out of trades is akin to modus operandi of the gambler.

I may be strange but I love the analysis. I see the trades proper as a
byproduct, which of course we need, however we can't force.

Thanks Gregg for your last post. It is one of many gems

I feel exactly the same way. I kind of underestimated the effort involved in following a pair all day long.

I'm trying to make some steps back and think on what is wrong with me
and I just noticed that when I spot a potential opportunity, I can't
look elsewhere, I just stay all day long, sometimes more than that, in
front of it, overanalyzing the whole thing.

That's a terrible mistake. It creates an emotionnal attachement to a
trade and you end up thinking "I waited so much time: it couldn't have
been for nothing"

You progressively lose you objectivity. And it drains so much energy...

And for sure you end up tiyng the success of the trade to your personnal confidence in what you do (sounds logical though...)

So much that when the trade you waited for all day long ends up miserably you feel miserable too.

This is an engrenage, a trap for novices i'm trying to get out of...

If your rectangle is above price, it must always be drawn from a low to the highest high on its right.

If your rectangle is below price, it must always be drawn from an high to the lowest low on its right.

To be tradeable, rectangles must cross lines drawn from highs and lows to the left
